content.text: Every software track sits on the same five basics: how a computer runs a program, your everyday tools and Git, data structures and algorithms, operating systems and networking. Learn them in that order, at working depth and next to real projects, before you go deep on any framework. Frameworks change every few years; these basics are what you keep.

Six months into a web framework course, a junior gets her first internship task: a report that matches every order to its customer. It works on her laptop and times out on the real data, because it searches a list inside a loop where a dictionary would answer at once. The same week she loses a day of work to a Git conflict she doesn't understand and an afternoon to a "connection refused" error that turns out to be the wrong port. The course taught her the framework. Nobody taught her what sits under it.
The common misconception

The belief is that you should pick a language or a framework first and get productive, and that computer science basics can wait until a job needs them. Smart people believe it for good reasons. Job ads list frameworks, not data structures. Tutorials get you building something visible in a weekend, while a chapter on processes feels like school. And plenty of good engineers never took a computer science degree.

Part of that is right: you don't need a degree, and you shouldn't study theory for a year before you write code. The wrong part is "later". The basics are cheapest to learn at the start, they carry over to every track you might pick, and without them every bug below the framework looks like magic.
What "the basics" really means
You need working knowledge, enough to reason about a bug, not to pass a university exam:

items.text: How a computer runs a program:
bits and bytes, memory, the CPU running instructions, and what compiled and interpreted mean. It explains why numbers overflow and why 0.1 + 0.2 isn't exactly 0.3.
the command line, an editor you can debug in, and Git. You use them every hour of every working day.
lists, hash tables, trees and graphs, and how to tell when code gets slow as data grows.
processes, threads, memory and files. Servers, phones and containers all run on these ideas.
IP addresses, ports, DNS, TCP and HTTP. Almost every program you write will talk to another one.

content.text: The stages from zero to your first track
The durations below are rough ranges for about 10 hours a week; at 20 hours, expect roughly half. The stages overlap: keep building while you read.

items.title: Stage 1: A first language and the machine under it

content.text: About 2–4 months at 10 hours a week.
Learn

one beginner-friendly language (Python or JavaScript; C if you follow CS50): variables, conditions, loops, functions, lists, dictionaries and reading error messages. Next to it, learn what happens underneath: bits, memory and the CPU running instructions.
Postpone
frameworks and the "best language" debate.
Build
a command-line program that saves its data to a file, such as a habit tracker or a quiz.
You're ready
when you can write a small program from an empty file without a video, and explain what a variable is in terms of memory.

items.title: Stage 2: The command line, an editor and Git

content.text: About 3–6 weeks at 10 hours a week, then daily practice.
Learn
to move around and run programs in a shell, to search and debug in your editor, and Git: commit, branch, merge, push to a remote and resolve a conflict.
Postpone
advanced scripting and history rewriting.
Build
a GitHub repository for your Stage 1 project with a README, change it on a branch and merge it back.
You're ready
when you commit small and often without thinking, and a merge conflict is a chore, not a panic.
About 2–4 months at 10 hours a week.
Learn

arrays, linked lists, hash tables, stacks, queues, trees and graphs; Big O notation; binary search, sorting, recursion and breadth-first search. This is what turns the timed-out report into one that runs.
Postpone
competitive programming and the hardest dynamic programming puzzles.
Build
a tool on real data, such as a word counter for a whole book or a shortest-route finder on a small map, and time it as the input grows.
You're ready
when you choose a data structure before you write the loop, and can say why.
About 1–3 months at 10 hours a week.
Learn
processes and threads, how memory is laid out (stack, heap, virtual memory), files, and concurrency: race conditions and locks.
Postpone
writing a kernel and the details of scheduling algorithms.
Build
a counter that several threads update at once: watch it give the wrong total, then fix it with a lock.
You're ready
when you can explain why two threads that change the same variable need coordination.
About 1–2 months at 10 hours a week.
Learn
IP addresses and ports, DNS, TCP and UDP, HTTP requests and responses, and what TLS adds.
Postpone
routing protocols and network engineering exams.
Build
a tiny HTTP client or server with your language's standard library, and watch a page load in the browser's Network tab.
You're ready
when you can walk through everything that happens between typing a URL and seeing the page.

items.title: Stage 6: Pick a track and keep the basics alive

content.text: Ongoing.
Learn

what each track does all day, pick one and follow its roadmap. Come back to the basics when the work asks: memory when a service leaks, algorithms when a page slows down, networking when calls time out.
Postpone
nothing new here; go deeper only when a real problem sends you.
Build
your track's first project, then write up one bug you solved with these basics.
You're ready to move on
once you've chosen a track and started its roadmap.
Books for each stage

rows.text: Code: The Hidden Language of Computer Hardware and Software
Remzi H. Arpaci-Dusseau, Andrea C. Arpaci-Dusseau
Randal E. Bryant, David R. O'Hallaron
James F. Kurose, Keith W. Ross

content.text: Two of these are older. Pro Git dates from 2014: its model of commits and branches still holds, but it switches branches with
git checkout
, while the official Git tutorial now uses
git switch

, so keep git-scm.com/docs open next to it. CS:APP's third edition is from 2015 and still the clearest account of memory, linking and performance; read it after OSTEP, not before. Two free courses fit the early stages too: Harvard's CS50x for Stages 1 and 3, and MIT's Missing Semester for Stage 2. The Kurose and Ross website also has free lectures and Wireshark labs for Stage 5.
Common mistakes

items.text: finishing course after course without building anything you designed yourself.
switching languages every few weeks, so you only ever learn the first chapter of each.
learning interview answers by heart instead of understanding why a hash table or a tree fits.
Treating Git as a save button:
one giant commit per week, and no branches until a job forces them on you.

content.text: After each stage, write a short note that explains one idea in your own words: why the threaded counter was wrong, or what DNS did before your page loaded. Two of the books and both free courses are legal to read online, so a pirated PDF is never the only way in.

blocks.title: The basics are not a new reason to wait

content.text: Don't finish every book before you build. One book per stage is enough, read next to a project. A learner who studies theory for a year without shipping anything has the same problem as one who skipped the theory.
How to show your work

Put every stage project on GitHub with a README that says what it does, how to run it and what you learned. Keep the commit history honest: small commits with clear messages show more than one perfect final upload. Write one short post per stage about a bug or an idea that surprised you.

content.text: Key takeaways

items.text: Every track needs the same five basics, from how a computer runs a program to networking.
Learn them in that order, at working depth, each one next to a small project you design yourself.
Plan in hours, not dates: at about 10 hours a week, the first five stages take roughly 7–14 months.
Pick your track once the basics are in place, and come back to them whenever a real bug sends you there.
